summary: The note reviews recent research and expert commentary on how sleep affects athletic performance and recovery. It covers muscle regeneration, sleep quality, the two-way link with exercise, the costs of sleep deprivation, hygiene strategies, wearable tech, diet, and sleep education. It concludes that sleep is as essential as diet, training, and mental preparation, though a gap remains between research and practice.
one_line: Experts and studies from 2023-2024 show sleep is essential for athletic performance and recovery, covering quality, deprivation, strategies, technology, diet, and education.
key_facts: David Randall, a circadian rhythm researcher at the University of California, said on October 5, 2023 that during sleep the body enters heightened anabolic activity focused on muscle regeneration and tissue restoration.
The sleep cycle includes REM (rapid eye movement) sleep and several phases of NREM (non-rapid eye movement) sleep, each significant for health and tissue repair.

Dr. Sofia Rodriguez, a sports medicine specialist, said in a September 25, 2023 webinar that athletes need deep, uninterrupted sleep because human growth hormone (HGH) is released then, vital for muscle growth and repair.

Sports physiologist Alexei Moroz wrote on September 15, 2023 that moderate to vigorous physical activity has a bidirectional relationship with sleep quality, with regular training often producing deeper, more restorative sleep.
Research at the Global Sports Science Summit on November 3, 2023 linked sleep deprivation to slower reaction times, decreased accuracy, diminished cognitive function, and increased injury risk.
A study led by Dr. Hailey Brooks, published December 1, 2023, recommended a consistent sleep schedule, a rest-conducive environment, and relaxation techniques before bed.
Dr. Brooks advised that coaches and sports health professionals should treat sleep as a priority for athletes.
Sports sleep coach Michael Saunders said on January 18, 2024 that wearable tech and sleep-monitoring apps help tailor sleep recommendations to each athlete's needs.

Nutritional biochemist Dr. Emma Clarkson said on February 12, 2024 that macronutrients and meal timing can significantly influence sleep quality, and good sleep affects appetite hormones and energy metabolism.
Sports psychologist James Keller said on March 22, 2024 that there is a growing movement to include sleep education as a fundamental component of athletic training programs.
The note says a gap remains between what sleep research suggests and the practices adopted by athletes and sports organizations.
